mobile_book_AUGUSTINE_CONF_EN.json.gz.author: Saint Augustine
mobile_book_AUGUSTINE_CONF_EN.json.gz.desc:
Augustine, bishop of Hippo in fourth-century North Africa, looks back over his own life. It is not addressed to the reader but to God from beginning to end, so that reading it feels like overhearing a long prayer.
Thirteen books. Books I to IX tell his life from birth through his conversion and the death of his mother Monica; Book X examines memory and his present self; Books XI to XIII meditate on the nature of time and on the opening chapter of Genesis.
He dwells at length on small sins, such as a boyhood theft, in order to dig out the root of sin itself, and recounts his years of ambition, wandering, and his mother’s tears. The confession of Book I, that the heart is restless until it rests in God, runs through the whole work.

mobile_book_BELGIC_CONF_EN.json.gz.desc:
Guido de Brès wrote this confession in French in 1561. Protestants in the Low Countries, then under persecution, meant it to show the authorities what they actually believed, and the tone of that defense is still audible in it.
Thirty-seven articles. It opens with the two ways God is known, then moves through Scripture and the Trinity, creation and providence, the fall and election, Christ and justification, the church with its offices and sacraments, the civil magistrate, and the last judgment.

E. M. Bounds, an American Methodist minister, on the preacher and prayer. Over twenty chapters he hammers a single point: power in preaching comes not from method or gift but from the man himself, and prayer is what makes the man.

mobile_book_CLEMENT_1ST_EN.json.gz.author: Clement of Rome
mobile_book_CLEMENT_1ST_EN.json.gz.desc:
A letter from the church at Rome to the church at Corinth, written about the year 96. It is among the earliest Christian writings to survive after the New Testament, and tradition ascribes it to Clement of Rome.
Sixty-six chapters. Facing a dispute in which Corinth had wrongly deposed its elders, it warns from a series of Old Testament figures what jealousy and division produce, then urges order, humility and repentance, and closes with a long prayer.
⚠ Before you read: this is an early church document, not Scripture. It quotes the Old Testament freely and refers directly to Paul’s first letter to the same church. Later writers used it to argue for the primacy of Rome, but the text itself is an exhortation between sister churches, and conclusions about church government differ between traditions, so it should not be read as proof for any one polity. Passages drawing on the natural lore of the day, such as the phoenix in chapter 25, are illustrations meant to explain resurrection, not scientific statements.

mobile_book_DIDACHE_EN.json.gz.author: Apostolic Fathers
mobile_book_DIDACHE_EN.json.gz.desc:
A short work whose title means "the teaching of the twelve apostles", generally dated to the late first or early second century. Its author is unknown. It is the oldest surviving manual of church life.
Sixteen brief chapters. The first part is moral instruction set out as the way of life and the way of death; the middle gives practical direction on baptism, fasting, prayer and the eucharist; the last treats how to test travelling prophets and teachers, the assembly on the Lord’s Day, and watchfulness for the Lord’s coming.
⚠ Before you read: this is an early church document, not Scripture. The final authority for faith and life is the Bible; read this as historical witness to how the generation just after the apostles lived out the word. Its specific rules, such as the mode of baptism or fasting on Wednesday and Friday, were the practice of one region in one era, not a standard binding on the church today. Authorship and date are still debated.

mobile_book_DIOGNETUS_EN.json.gz.desc:
A short letter answering the questions of a pagan inquirer named Diognetus. The author is unknown and it is usually dated between 130 and 200. It is often called the finest of the early Christian apologies.
Twelve short chapters. It takes up in turn who the Christians’ God is, why they love one another as they do, and why this faith appeared in the world only now.
⚠ Before you read: this is an early church document, not Scripture. Chapters 5 and 6, which compare Christians to the soul of the world and say that every foreign land is their homeland and every homeland a foreign land, and chapter 9 on the sweet exchange in which the righteousness of one justifies many sinners, are the best known. The single manuscript burned in the fire at Strasbourg in 1870, so the text survives only through earlier copies, and scholars discuss whether chapters 10 to 12 were joined on from another work. The criticism of Jewish ritual in chapters 3 and 4 belongs to the polemical manner of its time and should not be read as a judgement on Jewish people today.

mobile_book_HERMAS_SHEPHERD_EN.json.gz.desc:
A collection of visions, commandments and parables said to have been received by Hermas, a layman in Rome, in the first half of the second century. It was among the most widely read books in the early church.
Twenty-seven pieces in three groups: five visions, twelve commandments and ten parables. A figure called the Shepherd appears and explains the second and third groups.
⚠ Before you read: of the early church works held here, this is the one whose non-canonical status most needs stating. Its central question is whether repentance remains open to those who sin after baptism; the vision of the tower under construction and the parable of the elm and the vine are the best known parts. Some in the early church read it as Scripture, but the church did not finally receive it, and the Muratorian fragment already said it should be read privately but not publicly. Some passages, such as the strict claim that repentance after baptism is granted only once, sit awkwardly beside the Bible’s account of grace, so test it by Scripture as you read.

Letters written about the year 110 by Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, while he was being taken under guard to Rome to die. They were written on the road by a man facing execution, and the sentences are short and breathless.
Seven letters: to the churches at Ephesus, Magnesia, Tralles, Rome, Philadelphia and Smyrna, and one to Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna.
⚠ Before you read: this is an early church document, not Scripture. Its themes are the unity of the church, the insistence that Jesus was truly born, truly died and truly rose, and a bold faith in the face of martyrdom. The strong emphasis on the bishop is read differently by different traditions, so take it as the early church’s longing not to be scattered by heresy rather than as proof for a form of government. His plea that the Roman church not prevent his death is the cry of a man under persecution, not a teaching that one should seek martyrdom. Enlarged versions circulated later; the seven here are those scholars accept as genuine.

mobile_book_POLYCARP_PHIL_EN.json.gz.desc:
Two pieces connected with Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, remembered as a disciple of the apostle John: a letter he sent to the church at Philippi about the year 110, and the account of his death written by the church at Smyrna about 155.
Two parts. The letter quotes Paul freely and gives practical exhortation to elders, deacons, young men and wives in turn. The martyrdom follows the old bishop, who had served eighty-six years, from his arrest to the fire, told by eyewitnesses; it is the earliest such account we have.
⚠ Before you read: this is an early church document, not Scripture. The famous confession comes from here: eighty-six years I have served him, and he never did me wrong; how can I blaspheme my King who saved me? Miraculous details, such as the flame arching away from his body like a sail, mix eyewitness report with literary description, and their historical detail is debated. The closing note about gathering the martyr’s remains is also read differently by different traditions; it is safest to take it as affection for a teacher.

Dies ist ein zweimal tägliches Andachtsbuch von Charles Spurgeon, dem Pastor des Metropolitan Tabernacle in London. Über einer Bibelstelle entfaltet es auf etwa einer Seite Gedanken, die – egal welche Seite man aufschlägt – letztendlich immer zu Christus und seiner Gnade zurückführen.
Vom Morgen des 1. Januar bis zum Abend des 31. Dezember gibt es jeden Tag zwei Texte, insgesamt also siebenhundertundweiße. Da ein Text jeweils rund zweitausend Zeichen umfasst, eignet er sich gut für eine kurze Lektüre am Morgen und am Abend.
Der erste Text beginnt mit Josua 5,12, wo Israel durch die Wüste zieht und den Ertrag des Landes Kanaan isst, und das Jahr schließt mit dem letzten Text aus Jeremia 8,20: „Die Ernte ist vergangen, der Sommer ist dahin, und wir sind nicht gerettet“. Die Schriftstellen sind frei aus dem Alten und Neuen Testament gewählt, wobei Trost und Mahnung nebeneinanderstehen.

mobile_book_SPURGEON_ME_ES.json.gz.author: Charles Spurgeon
mobile_book_SPURGEON_ME_ES.json.gz.desc:
Es un devocional para dos veces al día, escrito por Charles Spurgeon, pastor del Tabernáculo Metropolitano de Londres. Cada lectura presenta un versículo bíblico y lo desarrolla en una página más o menos, y sin importar qué página abras, siempre te lleva de vuelta a Cristo y a su gracia.
Desde la mañana del 1 de enero hasta la noche del 31 de diciembre, son dos por día, un total de setecientas treinta y dos lecturas. Cada una tiene alrededor de dos mil caracteres, lo que la hace perfecta para una lectura breve por la mañana y por la noche.
La primera lectura abre con Josué 5:12, cuando Israel cruza el desierto y come del fruto de Canaán, y la última cierra el año con Jeremías 8:20: «Pasó la siega, terminó el verano, y nosotros no hemos sido salvos». Los textos se eligen tanto del Antiguo como del Nuevo Testamento, y el consuelo y la advertencia van de la mano.

Voici un recueil de méditations biquotidiennes écrit par Charles Spurgeon, pasteur du Metropolitan Tabernacle de Londres. Chaque page présente un verset biblique suivi d'un court développement, et peu importe la page où l'on s'ouvre, le propos ramène toujours à Christ et à sa grâce.
De matin le 1er janvier à soir le 31 décembre, cela fait deux textes par jour, soit un total de sept cent trente-deux lectures. Chaque texte compte environ deux mille caractères, ce qui convient parfaitement pour une lecture brève le matin et le soir.
Le premier texte s'ouvre sur Josué 5:12, au moment où les Israélites traversent le désert et mangent des produits du pays de Canaan, tandis que l'année se ferme sur Jérémie 8:20 : « La moisson est passée, l'été est fini, et nous ne sommes point sauvés ». Les textes sont choisis indifféremment dans l'Ancien et le Nouveau Testament, et la consolation y côtoie l'avertissement.

mobile_book_SPURGEON_ME_RU.json.gz.author: Чарльз Сперджен
mobile_book_SPURGEON_ME_RU.json.gz.desc:
Это сборник размышлений на каждый день — по два на сутки, — который написал Чарльз Сперджен, пастор лондонской Столичной скинии. В начале каждой заметки стоит стих из Писания, а дальше автор около страницы разворачивает его так, что на какой странице книгу ни откроешь, в итоге всё равно приходишь ко Христу и Его благодати.
Здесь собраны ровно семьсот тридцать два текста: по два на каждый день с утра 1 января и до вечера 31 декабря. Каждая заметка занимает около двух тысяч знаков, так что её как раз удобно прочитать утром или вечером за короткое время.
Книга открывается словами из пятой главы книги Иисуса Навина о том, как израильтяне ели плоды земли Ханаанской после скитаний по пустыне, а завершается на исходе года стихом из восьмой главы пророка Иеремии: «Жатва прошла, лето кончилось, а мы не спаслись». Тексты для размышлений берутся из Ветхого и Нового Заветов без разбору, и слова утешения идут рука об руку со строгим предостережением.

這部靈修集出自倫敦大都會會幕教堂的牧師查爾斯·司布真之手，一天兩篇，陪伴我們的早晚靈修。書中每篇都以一句經文開始，接著用大約一頁的篇幅來解說。無論我們隨手翻到哪一頁，字裡行間最終都會把我們的目光引向基督和祂豐盛的恩典。

Adam Clarke’s Commentary on the Bible, written by the early 19th-century Methodist theologian Adam Clarke, contains extensive research and deep insights covering the entire Scriptures.

descs.EN: John Gill's Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63) is a verse-by-verse commentary covering every chapter of Scripture. Gill, a Baptist minister and Hebraist, draws steadily on rabbinic sources, the Targums and the Talmud, and so supplies Jewish background that most English commentaries of his century leave untouched. His notes open with the biblical phrase itself and then unfold it clause by clause, which makes the work unusually easy to consult one verse at a time. Because it is complete rather than selective, it covers the narrative and legal books of the Old Testament that verse-level commentaries commonly pass over.

Matthew Henry's Commentary on the Whole Bible, written by the nonconformist minister Matthew Henry in the early 18th century, is a classic work celebrated for its practical and devotional application of the scriptures.

The commentary provides profound insights into the moral and instructional values of each passage, articulating the providence and grace of God throughout the Bible with a warm and eloquent writing style.
It remains widely regarded as a premier resource for fostering a godly life, serving as an essential companion for Bible students seeking both intellectual understanding and spiritual nourishment.
Despite covering the entire canon of Scripture, it remains highly accessible and practical, effectively guiding readers to connect biblical truths directly to their daily lives and personal faith.
